correctness.rationale: ARR and RRR reduce exactly to d/m and d/c on the stated lattice. Complete exact enumeration proves the lower boundary and first-layer count, while the persistent family follows from 2/(m-1)<1/2 for every m at least 6.

evidence: Cook and Sackett define ARR, RRR, and NNT and show that the same RRR can yield very different ARR/NNT values at different baseline risks.
Schechtman explicitly compares the same measures and reports that different measures can give different impressions.
The literature therefore strongly covers the mechanism and qualitative distinction, but not the finite lattice minimum.
broader_coverage.reasoning: Tie splitting and baseline-risk sensitivity do not imply the smallest sample size at which two positive-cell equal-arm trials receive opposite strict rankings. That requires a finite universal exclusion through arm size five.

originality.rationale: Prior clinical literature establishes the formulas and qualitative divergence between absolute and relative treatment summaries. The inspected sources and targeted searches did not state the sharp equal-arm positive-cell threshold of six, the exact two-pair first layer, or the persistent integer family.
residual_risks: The 1988 NEJM full article was not accessible through the checked route, although the later open full text by Cook and Sackett supplies the exact formulas and cites the 1988 source.
An unindexed educational example or software test could contain the same six-per-arm reversal.
Unequal arm sizes, zero cells, continuity corrections, or other treatment-effect summaries can have different minimal boundaries.

value.rationale: Absolute and relative risk reductions are canonical competing summaries in clinical evidence, and NNT is exactly the reciprocal absolute summary. The smallest nondegenerate equal-arm trial at which they make opposite strict comparative judgments is a natural finite benchmark. The result isolates baseline-risk standardization as the mechanism and remains present at every larger arm size.
